```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)
library(knitr)
pal <- c(navy = "#2b3a67", teal = "#2a9d8f", orange = "#e76f51",
         gold = "#e9c46a", grey = "#bbbbbb")
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 15))

res <- "results"
ords <- read_csv(file.path(res, "ordinations.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
perm <- read_csv(file.path(res, "permanova.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
scree <- read_csv(file.path(res, "scree.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
cs <- read_csv("../3-differential/results/contrast_summary.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
n_genes_outcome <- cs$n_sig[cs$contrast == "genes_by_outcome"]

ord_fig <- function(which_ord, colour_by, title = NULL, legend = "right") {
  d <- ords |> filter(ordination == which_ord)
  ggplot(d, aes(axis1, axis2, colour = .data[[colour_by]])) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.75, size = 2) +
    labs(x = "axis 1", y = "axis 2", colour = NULL,
         title = title %||% which_ord) +
    theme(legend.position = legend)
}
`%||%` <- function(x, y) if (is.null(x)) y else x
r2 <- function(tbl, trm) {
  v <- perm$R2[perm$table == tbl & perm$term == trm]
  scales::percent(v, 0.1)
}
```

## Yesterday: which feature differs? {.center}

Today: **how similar are two whole samples?**

. . .

One number per pair of samples, and then a picture of all of them at once.

## A distance matrix

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.6
set.seed(3)
n <- 12
m <- as.matrix(dist(matrix(rnorm(n * 4), n)))
as_tibble(m, .name_repair = ~ paste0("S", seq_along(.x))) |>
  mutate(row = paste0("S", row_number())) |>
  pivot_longer(-row) |>
  mutate(row = factor(row, paste0("S", 1:n)),
         name = factor(name, paste0("S", 1:n))) |>
  ggplot(aes(name, fct_rev(row), fill = value)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = pal[["navy"]]) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "distance") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
```

471 samples gives 110,685 pairs. Zero on the diagonal, symmetric, and that is
the whole object.

## Three ways to measure a distance {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
- **Bray-Curtis** on proportions. How much of the two communities overlaps.
  Abundant features dominate the answer.
- **Jaccard** on presence and absence. What share of the features present in
  either sample are present in both. Abundance is ignored entirely.
- **Aitchison**, which is Euclidean distance on centred log-ratios. Built for
  data where only the ratios between features mean anything.
:::

. . .

These are not interchangeable. They answer different questions.

## One pipeline, three knobs {.smaller}

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(microViz)
source("R/count_tables.R")

as_counts(table = "microbiome") |>
  tax_transform("identity", rank = "species") |>   # knob 1: the transform
  dist_calc("bray") |>                             # knob 2: the distance
  ord_calc("PCoA") |>                              # knob 3: the layout
  ord_plot(colour = "community")
```

. . .

| transform | distance |
|---|---|
| `"identity"` on proportions | `"bray"` |
| `"binary"` | `"jaccard"` |
| `"clr"` | `"euclidean"` |

: {tbl-colwidths="[50,50]"}

## The same samples, three distances

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 15
#| fig-height: 5
p1 <- ord_fig("species / Bray-Curtis", "community", "Bray-Curtis", "none")
p2 <- ord_fig("species / Jaccard", "community", "Jaccard", "none")
p3 <- ord_fig("species / Aitchison", "community", "Aitchison", "bottom")
(p1 + p2 + p3) &
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(anaerobe = pal[["orange"]], lactobacillus = pal[["teal"]]))
```

Three pictures of one table. Which would you put in a paper, and could you
defend it?

## What the axes are worth {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 3.9
scree |>
  filter(axis <= 8) |>
  ggplot(aes(factor(axis), variance_share, fill = table)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`species / Bray-Curtis` = pal[["teal"]],
                               `genes / Aitchison` = pal[["orange"]])) +
  facet_wrap(~table) +
  labs(x = "axis", y = "share of variation") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

The first two axes of the species ordination hold about
`r scales::percent(sum(scree$variance_share[scree$table == "species / Bray-Curtis" & scree$axis <= 2]), 1)`
of the variation. For the genes, about
`r scales::percent(sum(scree$variance_share[scree$table == "genes / Aitchison" & scree$axis <= 2]), 1)`.

## Colour the same plot by the thing you care about

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 14
#| fig-height: 5
a <- ord_fig("species / Bray-Curtis", "community", "by community", "bottom") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(anaerobe = pal[["orange"]], lactobacillus = pal[["teal"]]))
b <- ord_fig("species / Bray-Curtis", "outcome", "by birth outcome", "bottom") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(preterm = pal[["orange"]], term = pal[["navy"]]))
a + b
```

. . .

The left panel is obvious. The right panel is the one you actually want, and you
cannot see it.

## So stop squinting and test it {.smaller}

```{r}
#| eval: false
as_counts(table = "microbiome") |>
  tax_transform("identity", rank = "species") |>
  dist_calc("bray") |>
  dist_permanova(variables = c("community", "outcome", "time_point", "rnaseq_batch"),
                 n_perms = 999, by = "margin")
```

PERMANOVA asks: if I shuffled this label across samples, would the groups be
this far apart by chance?

. . .

`R2` is the share of the total variation that the label explains.

## The species table {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
perm |>
  filter(table == "species / Bray-Curtis", !term %in% c("Residual", "Total")) |>
  transmute(term, R2 = scales::percent(R2, 0.1), `F` = round(`F`, 1),
            p = p_value) |>
  kable(align = "lrrr")
```

::: {.incremental}
- Community type: `r r2("species / Bray-Curtis", "community")`. Enormous, and
  no surprise, since we defined it from this table.
- Visit: `r r2("species / Bray-Curtis", "time_point")`. These communities move
  over pregnancy.
- Birth outcome: `r r2("species / Bray-Curtis", "outcome")`. Significant and
  tiny.
- Sequencing batch of the **RNA**: `r r2("species / Bray-Curtis", "rnaseq_batch")`,
  not significant. Good. It should not matter here.
:::

## Now the gene table, same pipeline {.smaller}

```{r}
#| eval: false
as_counts(table = "rnaseq", min_count = 10, min_samples = 100) |>
  tax_transform("clr", rank = "symbol") |>
  dist_calc("euclidean") |>
  ord_calc("PCoA") |>
  ord_plot(colour = "community")
```

Three words changed. Everything else is the line you just ran.

## Three labels on the gene ordination

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 15
#| fig-height: 5
g1 <- ord_fig("genes / Aitchison", "community", "by community", "bottom") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(anaerobe = pal[["orange"]], lactobacillus = pal[["teal"]]))
g2 <- ord_fig("genes / Aitchison", "outcome", "by birth outcome", "bottom") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(preterm = pal[["orange"]], term = pal[["navy"]]))
g3 <- ords |> filter(ordination == "genes / Aitchison") |>
  ggplot(aes(axis1, axis2, colour = rnaseq_batch)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.75, size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(B1 = pal[["navy"]], B2 = pal[["gold"]])) +
  labs(x = "axis 1", y = "axis 2", colour = NULL, title = "by sequencing batch") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
g1 + g2 + g3
```

## The uncomfortable table {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
perm |>
  filter(!term %in% c("Residual", "Total")) |>
  transmute(table, term, R2 = scales::percent(R2, 0.1), p = p_value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = table, values_from = c(R2, p)) |>
  kable(align = "lrrrr")
```

. . .

In the gene table, the sequencing batch explains as much as the biology does,
and it is just as significant.

## What to do about that {.center}

::: {.incremental}
- You cannot see it in the ordination. You can only measure it.
- You can put it in the model: `~ rnaseq_batch + outcome`.
- You cannot fix it if it is confounded with your groups. Check first, always.
- You cannot check for it at all if nobody wrote the batch down.
:::

## Significant and small {.smaller}

Birth outcome in the gene table: `r r2("genes / Aitchison", "outcome")` of the
variation, p = 0.005.

. . .

Yesterday the same comparison gave `r scales::comma(n_genes_outcome)` significant genes.

. . .

Both are true. A great many genes shift slightly, and a slight shift in a great
many genes is a small share of a very large pile of variation.

. . .

Hold that thought until Friday.
